claim: Rod and cone photoreceptors are coupled by gap junctions.
source: Rod and cone photoreceptors are coupled by gap junctions (GJs), relatively large channels able to mediate both electrical and molecular communication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gap junctions can mediate both electrical and molecular communication.
source: Rod and cone photoreceptors are coupled by gap junctions (GJs), relatively large channels able to mediate both electrical and molecular communication.
evidence: This is a general property of gap junctions stated in the abstract.

claim: Rod–cone gap junctions are dynamically gated for dark/light adaptation.
source: Despite their critical location in our visual system and evidence that they are dynamically gated for dark/light adaptation, the full impact that rod–cone GJs can have on cone function is not known.
evidence: This is stated as existing evidence in the abstract.

claim: The initial level of rod input in mouse cones increased spontaneously after obtaining intracellular access.
source: We recorded the photovoltage of mouse cones and found that the initial level of rod input increased spontaneously after obtaining intracellular access.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the results.

claim: Fully coupled cones acquire a striking rod-like phenotype.
source: This process allowed us to explore the underlying coupling capacity to rods, revealing that fully coupled cones acquire a striking rod-like phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Calcium does not appear to be involved on the cone side of the junctional channels in the coupling process.
source: Calcium, a candidate mediator of the coupling process, does not appear to be involved on the cone side of the junctional channels.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with different calcium concentrations in whole cell recordings.

claim: The anatomical substrate is adequate for rod–cone coupling to play an important role in vision.
source: Our findings show that the anatomical substrate is adequate for rod–cone coupling to play an important role in vision and, possibly, in biochemical signaling among photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Rod–cone coupling may play a role in biochemical signaling among photoreceptors.
source: Our findings show that the anatomical substrate is adequate for rod–cone coupling to play an important role in vision and, possibly, in biochemical signaling among photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: In darkness, sparse single photon signals are relayed to retinal ganglion cells via a high gain/high convergence pathway formed by rods, rod bipolar cells, amacrine AII cells, and cone bipolar cells.
source: In darkness, sparse single photon signals are relayed to retinal ganglion cells via a high gain/high convergence pathway formed by rods, rod bipolar cells, amacrine AII cells, and cone bipolar cells (Nelson, 1982; Dunn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Rod signals can bypass rod bipolar cells and enter directly into the cone pathway.
source: However, rod signals can bypass rod bipolar cells and enter directly into the cone pathway (DeVries and Baylor, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The earliest opportunity for rod-to-cone crossover is represented by rod–cone gap junctions.
source: The earliest opportunity for this crossover is represented by rod–cone gap junctions (GJs) (Raviola and Gilula, 1973; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Gap junctions are assemblies of channels made by the docking of pairs of connexon hemichannels on adjacent cells, each formed by six connexin subunits.
source: GJs are assemblies of channels made by the docking of pairs of connexon hemichannels on adjacent cells, each formed by six connexin subunits.
evidence: This is general knowledge about gap junction structure.

claim: Cones contact nearby photoreceptors mainly at the tips of thin telodendria, which emerge from their synaptic pedicles.
source: Cones contact nearby photoreceptors mainly at the tips of thin telodendria, which emerge from their synaptic pedicles, where they express connexin isoform 36 (Cx36) (Lee et al., 2003; O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Cones express connexin isoform 36 (Cx36) at the tips of their telodendria.
source: Cones contact nearby photoreceptors mainly at the tips of thin telodendria, which emerge from their synaptic pedicles, where they express connexin isoform 36 (Cx36) (Lee et al., 2003; O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The connexin isoform expressed by rods has not been conclusively identified.
source: while the isoform expressed by rods has not been conclusively identified (Lee et al., 2003; Feigenspan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge with citations.

claim: Rod–cone junctional plaques are very small, each containing few connexon channels.
source: The rod–cone junctional plaques are very small, each containing few connexon channels (Raviola and Gilula, 1973)
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Rod signals were recorded in cat cones.
source: and although rod signals were recorded in cat (Nelson, 1977) and in macaque cones (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995, 1999; Hornstein et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Rod signals were recorded in macaque cones.
source: and although rod signals were recorded in cat (Nelson, 1977) and in macaque cones (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995, 1999; Hornstein et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The extent to which rod–cone coupling contributes to mammalian vision remains unclear.
source: the extent to which rod–cone coupling contributes to mammalian vision remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Psychophysical and electroretinographic experiments in humans detected putative correlates of rod–cone coupling.
source: psychophysical and electroretinographic (ERG) experiments, in humans, detected putative correlates of rod–cone coupling (reviewed by Sharpe and Stockman, 1999)
evidence: This is cited from a review in the literature.

claim: Ganglion cell and ERG recordings in mice lacking Cx36 supported the view that rod–cone coupling is relevant for dim light vision.
source: and ganglion cell and ERG recordings, in mice lacking Cx36, supported the view that rod–cone coupling is relevant for dim light vision (Deans et al., 2002; Volgyi et al., 2004; Abd-El-Barr et al., 2009; Seeliger et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Alternative mechanisms could explain the human psychophysical data on rod–cone coupling.
source: alternative mechanisms could explain the human data (Sharpe and Stockman, 1999)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Recordings in cone bipolar cells in Cx36 knockout mice suggested that rod–cone coupling plays a marginal role in rod signal flow.
source: and recordings in cone bipolar cells in Cx36 knockout mice suggested that rod–cone coupling plays a marginal role in rod signal flow (Pang et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Rod–cone gap junctions appear to be dynamically regulated.
source: Highly relevant to this debate is the fact that rod–cone GJs appear to be dynamically regulated
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on cited literature.

claim: Measurements of tracer diffusion in the outer rodent retina suggest that endogenous neuromodulators, light, and circadian clocks influence the level of coupling.
source: measurements of the extent of tracer diffusion in the outer rodent retina from the surface of a cut made with a razor blade (a technique referred to as 'cut-loading') (Ribelayga et al., 2008; Ribelayga and Mangel, 2010; Li et al., 2013), and ERG (Heikkinen et al., 2011) suggest that endogenous neuromodulators, light, and circadian clocks influence the level of coupling
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Cut-loading cannot discriminate between rod–rod, rod–cone and cone–cone gap junctions.
source: However, cut-loading cannot discriminate between rod–rod, rod–cone and cone–cone GJs
evidence: This is a limitation of the technique stated in the introduction.

claim: Cut-loading does not provide information on the absolute strength of coupling, but only on its relative changes.
source: and it does not provide information on the absolute strength of coupling, but only on its relative changes.
evidence: This is a limitation of the technique stated in the introduction.

claim: Direct proof of rod input in mouse cones was lacking prior to this study.
source: Here we investigated the first two of these questions in mouse, a mainstay of current retina research and one in which direct proof of rod input in cones is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mouse cones were only recently shown to be accessible for patch clamp recordings.
source: This important gap in our knowledge is explained by the fact that mouse cones were only recently shown to be accessible for patch clamp recordings (Cangiano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Mouse cones can be recorded with perforated patch clamp much more frequently than their numeric proportion of ∼3% of photoreceptors.
source: Cangiano et al. (2012) showed that mouse cones can be recorded with perforated patch clamp much more frequently than their numeric proportion of ∼3% of photoreceptors (Jeon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Data were collected from 74 cones in this study.
source: We present data from 74 cones.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Dim flashes (16.6 photons·µm−2) elicited large responses in rods while being too weak to stimulate cones.
source: dim flashes (16.6 photons·µm−2) elicited large responses in rods while being too weak to stimulate cones
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bright flashes (1570 and 3140 ph·µm−2) were sufficient to saturate rods for >1 s and evoke moderate responses in cones.
source: while bright flashes (a: 1570, b: 3140 ph·µm−2) were sufficient to saturate rods for >1 s and evoke moderate responses in cones.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The kinetics protocol consisted of sequences of three 520 nm flashes: dim/bright/dim flashes, with the third flash occurring at increasing delays.
source: Kinetics protocol made of sequences of three 520 nm (green, G) flashes, each consisting of dim/brighta/dim flashes, with the third flash occurring at increasing delays.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The spectral protocol consisted of sequences of 4 dim and bright flashes at 520 nm and 365 nm.
source: Spectral protocol made of sequences of 4 dim and brightb flashes at 520 nm (G) and 365 nm (UV).
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rod responses run down in kinetics during patch recordings.
source: Rod responses run down in kinetics during patch recordings (Cangiano et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from the literature and observed in the data.

claim: The kinetics rundown in rods alters their time course of recovery from saturating flashes.
source: a process that also alters their time course of recovery from saturating flashes (Figure 2A1, cf. black and gray records).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A1.

claim: Light response kinetics in rods can be stable for several hours in loose seal recordings.
source: as with this technique, light response kinetics can be stable for several hours (Figure 2A2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A2.

claim: The time course of the response to the kinetics protocol of rods in the initial minutes of patch recordings was similar to that in loose seal recordings.
source: The time course of the response to the kinetics protocol of rods in the initial minutes of patch recordings (n = 19, Figure 2A1, black records, taken before a significant amount of rundown occurred) was similar to that in loose seal recordings (n = 17), as shown in a graph of the normalized dim flash response amplitudes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Some cones responded only to the bright G flash, the expected behavior for uncoupled cones.
source: Some cones responded only to the brighta G flash (Figure 2C, top), the expected behavior for uncoupled cones (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The large majority of cones displayed responses to the first dim G flash, a plateau after the bright G flash, and a slow recovery of the dim flash response, similar to rods.
source: However, the large majority of cones displayed, similar to rods, responses to the first dim G flash, a plateau after the brighta G flash, and a slow recovery of the dim flash response (Figure 2C, middle/bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The similarity in the time course of recovery after the bright flash between rods and cones is strong evidence for the presence of rod input in cones.
source: This similarity in the time course of recovery after the bright flash emerges from comparing graphs of normalized dim flash response amplitudes during the kinetics protocol in rods (Figure 2B) and cones (Figure 2D, n = 11). This is strong evidence for the presence of rod input in cones.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: Cones showed a progressive increase in dim and bright flash peak response amplitudes and in the plateau during recording.
source: We observed in cones a progressive increase in dim and bright flash peak response amplitudes and in the plateau.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in multiple figures.

claim: The net change in cone response to the kinetics protocol was a scaled version of the typical rod response.
source: The net change in their response to the kinetics protocol was a scaled version of the typical rod response (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The progressive increase in coupling did not depend on the repeated exposure of the photoreceptor to light.
source: It did not depend on the repeated exposure of the photoreceptor to light, since it occurred also when single deliveries of the kinetics protocol were separated by several minutes of uninterrupted darkness (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cones acquired light sensitivity at intensities normally covered by rods during recording.
source: A response amplitude vs flash strength graph, obtained in two time ranges in the same cone (Figure 3B), highlights how cones acquired light sensitivity at intensities normally covered by rods.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The rate of increase in dim G flash response amplitude varied greatly among cones.
source: Its rate of increase varied greatly among cones.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most cones responded to dim G flashes already before patching, although response amplitudes were generally modest.
source: Based on these estimates, it appears that most cones responded to dim G flashes already before patching, although response amplitudes were generally modest when compared to those expressed during the recordings.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from Figure 4.

claim: Rod–cone junctional conductance is not hardwired, but it is modifiable in a wide range.
source: If the dim flash sensitivity of cones is due to rod input, then these observations imply that rod–cone junctional conductance is not hardwired, but it is modifiable in a wide range.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the text based on the observed data.

claim: A continuous light background of 6100 photons·µm−2·s−1 at 520 nm was rod saturating.
source: We attempted to isolate the pure cone component by saturating rods with a continuous light background of 6100 photons·µm−2·s−1 at 520 nm (for 5 min) based on ex vivo ERG data in mouse (Heikkinen et al., 2011) and our own rod data obtained with patch clamp and in loose seal. Control recordings confirmed that this particular background was, indeed, rod saturating (Figure 5A1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A1.

claim: Upon returning to darkness after a rod-saturating background, rod responses to the kinetics protocol recovered to near control levels after ∼2 min.
source: and showed that, upon returning to darkness, rod responses to the kinetics protocol recovered to near control levels after ∼2 min (n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A2.

claim: During a rod-saturating background, a sharp response to the bright G flash persisted in cones, while the slow plateau disappeared.
source: In contrast to rods, a sharp response to the brighta G flash persisted during the background, while the slow plateau disappeared as one would expect if it was generated by rods (Figure 5B1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B1.

claim: The sharp peak response in cones during a rod-saturating background did not represent a residual rod response.
source: The sharp peak did not represent a residual rod response, since increasing flash strength led to a marked increase in its amplitude (Figure 5B1, arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B1.

claim: When darkness was restored after a rod-saturating background, the dim and bright flash responses in cones recovered to near control levels in ∼2 min, in agreement with rods.
source: Importantly, when darkness was restored, the dim and bright flash responses recovered to near control levels in ∼2 min (n = 3), in agreement with what was observed in rods (cf. Figure 5 B2 with A2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B2.

claim: The peculiar features displayed by cones—a high light sensitivity and slow kinetics—may be entirely explained by rod input fed into the cone pathway through gap junctions.
source: This strongly suggests that the peculiar features displayed by cones—a high light sensitivity and slow kinetics—may be entirely explained by rod input fed into the cone pathway through GJs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experimental data.

claim: All cones stimulated with dim flashes displayed larger responses to G than to UV light.
source: We found that all cones stimulated with dim flashes displayed larger responses to G than to UV light (n = 20).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The behavior of cones displaying larger responses to G than to UV light for dim flashes was independent of their intrinsic spectral preference.
source: This behavior was independent of their intrinsic spectral preference in a wide range of G/UV ratios (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The dim flash responses in cones are driven by rods.
source: again supporting our hypothesis that dim flash responses in cones are driven by rods.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the spectral data.

claim: Both M- and S-dominant cones couple to rods.
source: Both M- and S-dominant cones couple to rods, as shown by a plot of the maximum dim G flash response amplitude observed in each cone vs its intrinsic spectral preference.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Three putatively pure S-cones were recorded in this study.
source: We also recorded from three putatively pure S-cones (i.e. blue cones; Figure 6C, leftmost circles)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The immunohistochemically derived frequency of pure S-cones is very low.
source: an important sample since the immunohistochemically derived frequency of these neurons is very low (Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: If dim and bright flash responses originated entirely in cones, their polarity should always be concordant.
source: If, on the other hand, dim and bright flash responses originated entirely in cones, their polarity should always be concordant.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the text.

claim: When cones were depolarized beyond the reversal potential of their photoresponse, bright flash responses reversed polarity while dim flash responses became smaller but did not reverse or became undetectable.
source: In all five cones tested, we observed that the brightb flash responses reversed in polarity (i.e., depolarizing) and actually became larger than in control conditions. In contrast, four of these cones had their dim flash responses reduced in amplitude to the point of being no longer distinguishable from noise, while the remaining one retained a small hyperpolarizing response (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: The dim and bright flash responses originate from separate electrotonic compartments.
source: This is not compatible with an origin of the dim and bright flash responses in the same electrotonic compartment
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the voltage-dependence experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Meclofenamic acid (MFA) is effective at gap junctions containing Cx36 in AII amacrine cells.
source: As a further confirmation of the results obtained thus far, we tested the specific GJ blocker meclofenamic acid (MFA), previously known to be effective at GJs containing Cx36 in AII amacrine cells (Pan et al., 2007; Veruki and Hartveit, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: 100 µM MFA had essentially no effect on rod recordings, except for a marginal reduction in light sensitivity attributed to normal rundown.
source: In three control rod recordings, 100 µM MFA was superfused with essentially no effect, except for a marginal reduction in light sensitivity that we attribute to the normal rundown observed during long rod recordings.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a control experiment.

claim: Superfusion with 100 µM MFA markedly reduced both dim flash responses and the slow plateau after bright flashes in cones.
source: In four cones tested, on the other hand, superfusion with 100 µM MFA markedly reduced both dim flash responses and the slow plateau after bright flashes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9A1.

claim: The slow pharmacodynamics of MFA observed in cone recordings confirmed a previous report in AII amacrine cells.
source: The slow pharmacodynamics of the blocker observed in our recordings (Figure 9A1, lower plot) confirmed a previous report in AII amacrine cells (Veruki and Hartveit, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 9A1, and cited from the literature.

claim: Junctional coupling transforms the sensitivity profile of the cone making it responsive to dim flashes, thereby widening its dynamic range.
source: Comparing graphs of response amplitude vs flash strength before and during perfusion with MFA in the same cone highlights how junctional coupling transforms the sensitivity profile of the cone making it responsive to dim flashes, thereby widening its dynamic range (Figure 9A2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9A2.

claim: Uncoupled cones displayed markedly decreased flash sensitivities compared to those found in Cangiano et al. (2012).
source: Uncoupled cones, including those recorded during superfusion with MFA (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), displayed markedly decreased flash sensitivities compared to those found in Cangiano et al. (2012)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uncoupled cone flash sensitivities approached those predicted using published estimates from functionally rodless retinas.
source: and approached those predicted using published estimates from functionally rodless retinas (Figure 1A,B, simulated curves on the right; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Rod–cone coupling is expressed near body temperature.
source: As the experiments shown so far were performed near room temperature, we verified the occurrence of rod–cone coupling also near body temperature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 10.

claim: Rods showed faster kinetics near body temperature compared to room temperature.
source: The response to the kinetics protocol of a rod recorded in loose seal (Figure 10A) showed, as expected, faster kinetics near body temperature (cf. Figure 2A2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: In all five cones recorded near body temperature, dim G flash responses and plateaus after bright G flashes were observed.
source: In all five cones recorded near body temperature, we observed dim G flash responses (0.28, 0.32, 0.43, 1.47, and 1.70 mV) and plateaus after brighta G flashes
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: MFA (100 µM) abolished both dim flash responses and plateaus following the bright flash in a cone recorded near body temperature.
source: In one of these cones, we tested the effect of the GJ blocker MFA (100 µM): both dim flash responses and plateaus following the brighta flash were abolished, leaving behind a fast response to the brighta flash (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The progressive increase in rod–cone coupling was not evoked by slicing of the retina but rather by some interaction between the recording pipette and the cone and/or its nearby rods.
source: The progressive increase in rod–cone coupling observed in our recordings was not evoked by slicing of the retina but rather by some interaction between the recording pipette and the cone and/or its nearby rods: cones were patched not earlier than 1 hr after slicing and in some cases, after several hours, yet in most cones, initial coupling upon sealing was weak, developing rapidly thereafter (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from Figure 4.

claim: The spontaneous increase in coupling was expressed in perforated patch recordings, even in combination with EGTA in the pipette solution.
source: In four of five cones recorded with 1 mM EGTA in the pipette (EGTA zero Ca2+ perforated patch solution), we observed the same progressive increase in coupling (Figure 4, blue lines).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The spontaneous increase in coupling is not dependent on diffusion of Ca2+ between the cell and the pipette.
source: These results effectively rule out an involvement of pipette Ca2+ but leave open the possibility that an increase in free [Ca2+]i in the cone, promoted by the pipette, drives the coupling process.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the EGTA experiments.

claim: Whole cell recordings with buffered pipette Ca2+ levels made in close proximity to the gap junctions strongly suggest that changes in free [Ca2+]i in cones are not responsible for the expression of the coupling increase.
source: Second, our recordings in whole cell patch clamp with buffered pipette Ca2+ levels, made in close proximity to the GJs, strongly suggest that changes in free [Ca2+]i in cones are not responsible for the expression of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the whole cell experiments shown in Figure 11.

claim: In two of three cones recorded with an EGTA low Ca2+ whole cell solution, rod coupling increased rapidly in the first minutes of recording.
source: We recorded from three cones with an EGTA low Ca2+ whole cell solution (50 nM free [Ca2+]i; see 'Materials and methods'), of which only one had weak coupling to rods upon breaking the patch. In two of the three cones, rod coupling increased rapidly in the first minutes of recording (Figure 11A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 11A.

claim: All three cones recorded with a BAPTA low Ca2+ whole cell solution were initially uncoupled but rapidly increased their coupling to rods up to moderate levels.
source: Further, we recorded from three cones with a BAPTA low Ca2+ whole cell solution (50 nM free [Ca2+]i) to rule out an involvement of fast and localized calcium transients. While all three cones were initially uncoupled, they rapidly increased their coupling to rods up to moderate levels (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 11B.

claim: High calcium on the cone side is not required for the expression of the progressive increase in coupling.
source: Since in all these experiments free calcium in the pedicle was buffered at very low levels compared to those normally present in darkness (∼2 µM spatially averaged: Szikra and Krizaj, 2006), we conclude that high calcium (on the side of the cone) is not required for the expression of the progressive increase in coupling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the whole cell experiments.

claim: No obvious favoring effect on coupling of high calcium emerged from cones recorded with an EGTA high Ca2+ whole cell solution.
source: Thus, no obvious favoring effect on coupling of high calcium emerged from this group of cones.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the high calcium experiments shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The possibility that what is interpreted as rod input could instead represent a change in cone phototransduction can be rejected.
source: The possibility that what we interpret as rod input could instead represent a change in cone phototransduction can be rejected, as it is contradicted by our findings that: (i) the GJ blocker MFA abolished rod-like responses in cones, (ii) dim and bright flash responses have different reversal potentials, (iii) in many cones, dim and bright flash responses (delivered after a rod-saturating pre-flash) display opposite spectral preferences.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Most mouse cones express both S and M opsins, with their expression ratio varying along the dorsoventral axis of the retina.
source: Except for a small number of pure S-cones (i.e. blue cones), most mouse cones reportedly express both S and M opsins, with their expression ratio varying along the dorsoventral axis of the retina (Applebury et al., 2000; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Daniele et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: M-opsin has a prominent secondary absorption peak in the near UV region (the β-band).
source: Moreover, any pure M-cones would respond to UV light since M-opsin has a prominent secondary absorption peak in the near UV region (the β-band; Govardovskii et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Both S-dominant cones (known to be mid and ventrally located) and M-dominant cones (dorsally located) are able to couple strongly to rods.
source: We could however conclude that both S-dominant cones (known to be mid and ventrally located) and M-dominant cones (dorsally located) are able to couple strongly to rods (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on Figure 6C.

claim: There is some evidence in macaque that blue cones form fewer junctional contacts with rods compared to other cone types.
source: Interestingly, there is some evidence in macaque that blue cones form fewer junctional contacts with rods compared to other cone types (O'Brien et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Each cone in mouse forms junctional contacts with an average of 32 rods.
source: Each cone in mouse forms junctional contacts with an average of 32 rods (Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The only measurement in mammals of the transjunctional conductance was made in rod–cone pairs of the cone-dominated ground squirrel retina.
source: To our knowledge, the only measurement in mammals of the transjunctional conductance was made in rod–cone pairs of the cone-dominated ground squirrel retina (legend of supplementary Figure 6 in Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The average transjunctional conductance in ground squirrel rod-cone pairs was 121 pS, corresponding to ∼20 open homotypic Cx36 channels.
source: Assuming that their average value of 121 pS for coupled pairs (corresponding to ∼20 open homotypic Cx36 channels; Moreno et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Multiplying the average transjunctional conductance by a rod–cone convergence of 32 gives a summed junctional conductance of ∼3900 pS.
source: multiplying it by a rod–cone convergence of 32 gives a summed junctional conductance of ∼3900 pS.
evidence: This is a calculation stated in the discussion.

claim: A 4 mV hyperpolarization in rods relative to a maximally coupled cone would be sufficient to draw from it an overall junctional current of ∼16 pA.
source: This would imply that a 4 mV hyperpolarization in rods relative to a maximally coupled cone would be sufficient to draw from it an overall junctional current of ∼16 pA—a very large value as it is comparable to estimates of the circulating current in mouse cones in darkness (Nikonov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a calculation stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: The data are compatible with the limited available evidence on transjunctional conductance.
source: Therefore, our data are compatible with the limited available evidence.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: In the area centralis of the cat retina, ∼48 rods converge on each cone.
source: in the area centralis of the cat retina, Smith et al. (1986) estimated a convergence of ∼48 rods on each cone
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: In the peripheral retina of macaque, ∼25 rods converge on each cone.
source: while in the peripheral retina of macaque, ∼25 rods converge on each cone (O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Rods did not respond appreciably to bright cone-stimulating flashes delivered during a rod-saturating background, or following rod-saturating pre-flashes.
source: We did not observe cone signals entering rods through GJs, since rods did not respond appreciably to bright cone-stimulating flashes delivered during a rod-saturating background, or following rod-saturating pre-flashes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Rod–cone divergence in mouse is small (∼1).
source: Two possible explanations for this are: (i) rod–cone divergence in mouse is small (∼1; Tsukamoto et al., 2001)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: A previous study in macaque reported a twofold speed-up of rod signals as they flow into cones through gap junctions.
source: A previous study in macaque reported a twofold speed-up of rod signals as they flow into cones through GJs (Hornstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: In patched cones, the time to peak (TTP) of dim flash responses was 197 ms (SD 35, n = 24), significantly shorter than the 258 ms (SD 25, n = 23) of rods recorded in loose seal.
source: We confirmed this in mouse, observing however a much less dramatic effect: in patched cones, the time to peak (TTP) of dim flash responses was 197 ms (SD 35, n = 24), significantly shorter (p<0.0001) than the 258 ms (SD 25, n = 23) of rods recorded in loose seal
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental data.

claim: A progressive increase in junctional coupling as a specific consequence of patch recording was observed in other studies targeting Cx36-expressing neurons.
source: As mentioned in the 'Results', a progressive increase in junctional coupling as a specific consequence of patch recording was observed in other studies targeting Cx36-expressing neurons, including heterologous expression systems (Zoidl et al., 2002; Del Corsso et al., 2012) and rat retinal amacrine AII cells (Veruki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Veruki et al. found that high resistance (fine-tipped) electrodes prevent the coupling increase in AII amacrine cells, suggesting a dialysis process.
source: Veruki et al., recording in whole cell mode, found that high resistance (i.e., fine-tipped) electrodes prevent the coupling increase, suggesting a dialysis process.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Del Corsso et al. surmised that an increase in intracellular Ca2+ triggers the coupling increase during whole cell recordings in neuroblastoma cells in vitro.
source: Del Corsso et al. (2012) surmised that an increase in intracellular Ca2+ triggers the coupling increase during whole cell recordings in neuroblastoma cells in vitro.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Del Corsso et al. reported that the coupling increase did not occur when recording in perforated patch clamp mode with amphotericin-B, implicating pipette-cell dialysis.
source: Moreover, they reported that the coupling increase did not occur when recording in perforated patch clamp mode with amphotericin-B, again implicating pipette-cell dialysis.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: In cones, the spontaneous increase in coupling is not dependent on diffusion of Ca2+ between the cell and the pipette.
source: First, in cones, this phenomenon is not dependent on diffusion of Ca2+ between the cell and the pipette, as the spontaneous increase in coupling was expressed in perforated patch recordings, even in combination with EGTA in the pipette solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data.

claim: Diffusible messenger molecules in cones are not necessarily involved in the coupling increase process.
source: Moreover, since the progressive increase in coupling was observed both when preserving the intracellular environment of the cone (perforated patch recordings) and when intentionally dialyzing it (whole cell recordings), a general tentative conclusion may be advanced: diffusible messenger molecules in cones are not necessarily involved in the process.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental data.

claim: A previous study on macaque reported that Neurobiotin injected in cones at the end of perforated patch recordings diffused preferentially to rods located under the recording pipette.
source: Evidence for a primary trigger mechanism can be found in a previous study on macaque (Hornstein et al., 2005), which reported that Neurobiotin injected in cones at the end of perforated patch recordings diffused preferentially to rods located under the recording pipette
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Hornstein et al. suggested that the electrode might alter the coupling efficiency of the rod–cone junctions by mechanical disturbance.
source: leading them to suggest that 'the electrode might alter the coupling efficiency of the rod–cone junctions by mechanical disturbance'.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Coupling would be promoted by stretch/deformation of the rods adjacent to the recorded cone.
source: In this scenario, and taking into account the arguments given above, coupling would be promoted by stretch/deformation of the rods adjacent to the recorded cone.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: Del Corsso et al. found a Ca2+-mediated enhancement in the activity of calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), which would lead to phosphorylation of Cx36 and increased channel conductance.
source: With regard to the downstream pathways, Del Corsso et al. (2012) found in their heterologous expression system a Ca2+-mediated enhancement in the activity of calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), which would lead to phosphorylation of Cx36 and increased channel conductance.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: CaMKII was recently found to participate in the physiological regulation of Cx36 in AII amacrines.
source: Interestingly, CaMKII was recently found to participate in the physiological regulation of Cx36 in AII amacrines (Kothmann et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: CaMKII may play a role in photoreceptors, on the rod side of rod–cone gap junctions.
source: raising the possibility that this kinase may play a role also in photoreceptors, on the rod side of rod–cone GJs (see above).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: At the start of the recordings, most cones were modestly coupled to rods relative to their full coupling potential.
source: At the start of the recordings, we found most cones modestly coupled to rods relative to their full coupling potential, although we observed strong initial coupling in a limited sample (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on Figure 4.

claim: Candidate regulators of rod–cone gap junctions in mammals include circadian synthesis and release of melatonin, dopamine, and adenosine.
source: Candidate regulators of rod–cone GJs in mammals are (references in the 'Introduction'): (i) the circadian synthesis and release of the endogenous retinal neuromodulators, melatonin, dopamine, and adenosine, whereby coupling would be stronger at night when melatonin levels are high
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with references to the introduction.

claim: Most mouse strains, including the C57BL/6 used in this study, have deficits in melatonin synthesis.
source: most mouse strains, including the C57BL/6 used here, have deficits in melatonin synthesis (Roseboom et al., 1998)
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The low level of coupling estimated for unperturbed cones may be related to the melatonin synthesis deficit in C57BL/6 mice.
source: it is therefore possible that the low level of coupling that we estimated for our unperturbed cones may be related to this deficit and that full blown coupling, of the strength emerging during our recordings, is recruited in melatonin-competent mouse strains at night
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: Acute light exposure would inhibit rod-cone coupling.
source: (ii) acute light exposure, acting on the same neuromodulators and possibly also locally in the photoreceptors, which would inhibit coupling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on literature references.

claim: A major discrepancy in the literature is the lack of effect of light and dopamine on rod–cone coupling studied with patch clamp in macaque.
source: Unfortunately, unresolved discrepancies persist in the literature, a major one being the lack of effect of light and dopamine on rod–cone coupling studied with patch clamp in macaque (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1999).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Gap junctions play a dual role as conduits of electrical signals and of intracellular molecules.
source: One should recollect that GJs play a dual role, for example, conduits of electrical signals and of intracellular molecules.
evidence: This is general knowledge about gap junctions.

claim: Cx36 is critically involved in neuronal responses to injury and disease.
source: Cx36, in particular, is critically involved in neuronal responses to injury and disease (Belousov and Fontes, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The existence of a large degree of gap junction-mediated anatomical convergence from rods to cones is not peculiar to the mouse.
source: The existence of a large degree of GJ-mediated anatomical convergence from rods to cones is not peculiar of the mouse, since it has been found in other rod-dominated mammalian retinas including the peripheral retina of macaque.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on cited literature.

claim: The findings on the functional impact of rod input in mouse cones may have broad relevance, supporting the possibility that rod–cone coupling plays a significant role in vision and/or in biochemical signaling between photoreceptors.
source: It follows that our findings on the functional impact of rod input in mouse cones may have broad relevance, supporting the possibility that rod–cone coupling plays a significant role in vision and/or in biochemical signaling between photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: Adult C57BL/6J mice were raised on a 12/12 hr light cycle.
source: Briefly, adult C57BL/6J mice, raised on a 12/12 hr light cycle, were dark-adapted for 3–5 hr and recorded during the subjective late afternoon of the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were dark-adapted for 3–5 hr before recording.
source: Briefly, adult C57BL/6J mice, raised on a 12/12 hr light cycle, were dark-adapted for 3–5 hr and recorded during the subjective late afternoon of the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Recordings were performed during the subjective late afternoon of the animal.
source: Briefly, adult C57BL/6J mice, raised on a 12/12 hr light cycle, were dark-adapted for 3–5 hr and recorded during the subjective late afternoon of the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Dissection and slicing were done in chilled bicarbonate-buffered Ames' medium under dim far red illumination.
source: Dissection and slicing were done in chilled bicarbonate-buffered Ames' medium (A1420; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) under dim far red illumination.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Blind patch recordings of photoreceptors were performed at 24°C or 36°C in Ames' medium.
source: Blind patch recordings of photoreceptors (at 24°C or 36°C) were also done in Ames' medium and targeted sections of retinal slices (250 µm) corresponding to both the central and peripheral retina.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The position of recordings along the dorsoventral axis of the retina could not be identified.
source: We could not identify the position of our recordings along the dorsoventral axis of the retina.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Perforated patch clamp and whole cell recordings were obtained from both rods and cones.
source: Perforated patch clamp and whole cell recordings were obtained from both rods and cones, while loose seal recordings could be obtained only from rods.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Loose seal recordings could be obtained only from rods.
source: Perforated patch clamp and whole cell recordings were obtained from both rods and cones, while loose seal recordings could be obtained only from rods.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The absorption peaks of rhodopsin, M-opsin, and S-opsin in mouse are at 498 nm, 508 nm, and 359 nm, respectively.
source: For reference, in mouse, the absorption peaks of rhodopsin, M-opsin, and S-opsin are at 498 nm, 508 nm, and 359 nm, respectively (Sun et al., 1997; Yokoyama et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.
